INDRA — The Story of the King of Heaven
GODS BEFORE GODS
Gods before the gods

INDRA — The Story of the King of Heaven

Book One · First Volume
Mahesh Gupta

What is this series about?

Gods Before Gods — Gods before the gods. Long before the great temples of Vishnu and Shiva, people sang songs of the sky, of fire, of dawn, and of storm. Those songs came to be called the Veda, and the gods they called upon — Indra, Agni, Surya, Vayu, Varuna, Usha — they are the gods of this series. The old gods, whose stories were sung first of all.

Each volume in this series tells one god's whole life — from birth to today, as a single story, start to finish.

And one promise: This book is not for worship, but for understanding. We are not saying, worship these gods — we want to explain why people worshipped them. So every god is shown honestly: his great deeds first and foremost, and his weaknesses not hidden either — but they are not the spine of the story. Greatness too, and mistakes too, both together.

This book is for those meeting these gods for the first time — children and families who know the names but not the stories — and for those too who know the names, but have never heard the whole story.

How each book is made

One god's life in six rooms: Where did he come from? · Companions and weapons · What did he do? · Where did he go wrong? · In later stories · Where is he today?
Along the way there are boxes that tell you “good things”, and at the end of every part, Pause and think , and where stories are told differently, a footnote — one main story, the other versions in the notes.

So come — first meet Indra, king of the gods of the oldest hymns.

Who is Indra? — an introduction

The sky went dark — and then they came

First look at the sky. Clouds began to thunder like drums, the wind seemed to hold still, and whether god or man — every gaze rose upwards. (Slowly, holding your breath) The world seemed to stand holding its breath — something great was about to happen.

And then they came — riding the white elephant Airavata, a shining vajra in hand, in a golden crown. (Raising your voice, proudly) Behind them the rain broke loose. This is Indra's first glimpse — this is how a king arrives, so that even the sky welcomes him.

The rishis have called him with great respect — Devaraja, king of the gods; Vajradhari, the one who holds the vajra; Shatakratu, performer of a hundred yajnas; and Purandara, breaker of forts. And this praise is not for nothing — he freed the held-back water, he gives the very rain every field depends on, he is the king behind whom the gods themselves march into war, and whoever calls upon him, he protects.

Indra is easy to recognise: a golden crown on his head, a shining vajra in his hand, and his mount, the white elephant Airavata. When clouds thunder in the sky, people say — that is Indra's voice. And when rain falls, that is Indra's gift. Understand how great a god Indra was from just one thing: nearly every fourth verse of the Rigveda calls upon him.

Indra's marks — at a glance

Vajra — Indra's shining weapon, swift as lightning.
Airavata — his white elephant, his mount and companion.
Amaravati / Svarga — the gods' world, where Indra rules.
Storm clouds — deep blue clouds, thunder and rain — the mark of Indra's world.

So know this — you have just met someone great. This is Indra — Devaraja, Vajradhari, king of the sky. Now hear his story, from the start, to the beat of drums.

A word about the series

This book is not for worship, but for understanding

This series is named — Gods before the gods. That is, those old gods whose songs were sung long before the great temples of Vishnu and Shiva were built. Indra was the first and greatest among them.

This book's point is clear, and it must be said right at the start: This book is not for making you worship, but for making you understand. We will praise Indra so that we can understand — why people worshipped him, why they sang his songs, and why, seeing the first cloud before the rain, they took his name.

And we will look at Indra honestly — as he is. His great deeds will stay in the middle, greatest and brightest. His mistakes will be told too — honestly, but briefly. Neither will mistakes be hidden, nor will they become the whole story. (In a clear, slow voice) Because truly knowing someone is the real appreciation of him.

This book's rooms

  1. Where did he come from? — birth, title, and heaven's capital, Amaravati.
  2. Indra's companions and weapons — Airavata, the vajra, his powers and treasures.
  3. What did he do? — Vritra, the war of the ten kings, and the war with Ravana.
  4. Where did he go wrong? — pride, Ahalya, and Karna's armour.
  5. In later stories — Indra in the Ramayana, the Mahabharata, and the Bhagavata.
  6. Where is he today? — Indra in rain songs, festivals, and names.

🌿 Pause and think — Introduction

What is the difference between appreciating someone and worshipping them? Can you appreciate a person who has some faults too — like a favourite player or teacher? This way of seeing will stay with us through the whole book.

Room One — Where did he come from?

Son of the sky, a warrior from birth

The Rigveda's songs say that Indra is the sky's son. He did not come as an ordinary child — he was a warrior from birth. (In wonder, softly) They say, the moment he was born he asked for soma — the sacred juice that gave the gods strength — and then picked up the vajra.

In other words, the very first moment of Indra's story tells us what he came for: to protect the weak, and to cut through darkness and open a path.

And now the layer of history — this is important to understand

Thousands of years ago, people living by the rivers sang songs as they looked at the sky, the fire, the dawn, and the storm. Those songs came to be called the Veda, and those who sang them came to be called rishis — wise seers.

Long before the great temples of Vishnu and Shiva were built, people prayed to these very sky-gods. There was Agni for fire, Usha for dawn, and for storm and rain the king was — Indra. He was king of the very first gods of all.

Glossary

Veda — a collection of very old sacred songs.
Rishi — the wise ones who sang these songs and kept them safe.
Yajna — a prayer that calls the gods by offering into fire.
Svarga — the gods' world, where Indra rules.

Room One — Where did he come from? · continued

Indra — a person, or a title?

Here is an interesting thing, without which Indra's story stays half-told. Indra is both a person and a title.

The Indra whose story is in this book has his own name too — Shakra, and another name — Purandara, breaker of forts. He is the Indra of our age. But heaven's throne is no one person's property. Ages change, and the one who sits on the throne can change too.

Think of it like a school, where “principal” is a post — the person changes, the post remains. In the same way, “Indra” is the post of heaven's king, and in our age Shakra sits in that post.

Nahusha — who sat on the throne and fell

Once it happened that Indra's post fell vacant, and a human king — Nahusha — was made king of heaven for a time. At first Nahusha ruled well. But slowly pride grew in his mind.

His pride grew so great that he insulted the rishi Agastya — he even told him to carry his palanquin, and in anger kicked him with his foot. (Slowly, like a warning) Right there, his fall came. Agastya cursed him, and Nahusha fell from heaven and became a serpent.

The rishis said — “One who holds a post with pride is brought down by the post itself.”

Room One — Where did he come from? · continued

And Bali — the future Indra

Nahusha's story has another end too — a promise. They say that in a coming age, called the Savarni manvantara, Bali will sit on heaven's throne.

This is the same Bali — the asura-king whose story you have already read in this series' Vamana tale. There, Vishnu, as Vamana, asked Bali for three steps of earth, and Bali gave away everything he had — his kingdom, his pride, everything. So great in giving, and so true to his word, that he was promised the post of the future Indra.

See how the stories join each other: the Bali who lost his kingdom in the Vamana tale will one day become king of heaven. (In wonder, smiling) Losing, too, is sometimes the preparation for winning — you only need to know how to keep your word.

📜 What is a manvantara?

In the old stories, time is divided into great ages, called manvantaras. Every manvantara has its own Manu, and its own Indra too. Our manvantara is the Vaivasvata manvantara, whose Indra is Shakra. The next great age will be called Savarni — and its Indra will be Bali.

Amaravati — the golden city, the Sudharma assembly, the Nandana gardens, the Parijata tree, the Gandharvas' music, and Indra on his Airavata.
Room One — Where did he come from? · Amaravati

Amaravati — the golden city

The city where Indra rules is named Amaravati. They say it was built by the gods' craftsman Vishvakarma — gates of gold, palaces studded with jewels, and such a blaze that the eyes dazzle.

In the middle of the city is Sudharma — the gods' assembly. There the gods sit and consider the world's affairs: when the rain should fall, when the river should be freed, whose protection is needed when. Indra sits in the middle there — not like a king, but like the head of an assembly.

And outside the city are the Nandana gardens — gardens where spring lasts forever. There the flowers never fade, and music always floats in the air.

Someone asked — “What is the most beautiful thing in heaven?” The answer came — “Its music, and the fragrance of its flowers.”

Room One — Where did he come from? · Amaravati

Parijata, the apsaras, and one honest truth

Two trees are the most famous in the Nandana gardens — Parijata, whose flowers' fragrance travels far and wide, and Kalpavriksha, of which they say that whatever you ask for beneath it, you receive. There the Gandharvas sing, and the apsaras — Urvashi, Menaka — dance.

Airavata has his own place in Amaravati, and so does the white horse Ucchaishrava. Everything is beautiful, everything is rich — but here one honest thing must also be said, because it is this very thing that makes Indra's story true.

Heaven is earned by punya — good deeds — and when the punya runs out, heaven too runs out. The Gita says (9.21) that when punya fades, even heaven's dwellers return. So heaven is not a forever place; it is a fruit, earned by deeds and left behind when those deeds are complete.

🌿 Pause and think — Where did he come from?

If even heaven does not last forever, then what lasts forever? Is there something — like a good deed done, or a helping hand — that does not slip away with time? And from the stories of Nahusha and Bali, what did you learn about a post and the person who holds it?

Room Two — Indra's companions and weapons

Airavata — the elephant like a cloud

Every king has a mount, but Indra's mount is no ordinary elephant. Airavata is the king of elephants — white, like a rain cloud; vast, like a walking mountain; and so gentle that even children are not afraid of him.

Airavata's story is joined to the churning of the ocean — the same churning whose story has already been told in an earlier book of this series. When the gods and asuras churned the ocean together, many treasures came out of it. One of them was Airavata — the white elephant, who was given to Indra. We will not tell that churning again here; just know that Airavata is the gift of that great event.

Airavata is not only a mount — he is Indra's companion. In war he carries Indra along, and in peace he wanders the gardens of heaven. They say, when white clouds gather in the sky, people say — Airavata is on the move.

Indra said — “My vajra is my strength, but Airavata is my company. Strength walks alone; company carries you far.”

Airavata — white as a cloud, adorned with gold ornaments, king of elephants.
Room Two — Indra's companions and weapons

The vajra — the weapon of lightning

Now the weapon without which Indra's picture is incomplete — the vajra. The gods' skilled craftsman Tvasta forged it for Indra. Thick in the middle, a strong cylinder — so thick that a fist closes fully around it — with points curling out on both sides. This is the form you will see in every picture in this book.

What is the vajra's power? It splits mountains, breaks dams, and frees held-back water. It is lightning itself — the sky's flash that cuts the darkness in a single moment. Against Vritra too this same vajra struck, and in the war of the ten kings this same vajra will break the river's dam.

And one more thing: the vajra, even when it leaves Indra's hand, returns to him. (Slowly, with respect) As if a good weapon knows its master.

📜 The vajra's other story (note)

There is another famous story too: that the vajra was made from the bones of the rishi Dadhichi — he gave up his body to protect the gods. In this book the main story stays Tvasta's; Dadhichi's story is recorded here as a different story, not blended with the main one.

The vajra — a thick cylinder in the middle, points curling out on both sides; lightning itself in form.
Room Two — Indra's companions and weapons

His powers — rain, thunder, and a thousand eyes

Indra's greatest power is the simplest — he is lord of rain and thunder. When he wishes, clouds gather; when he raises the vajra, lightning flashes; and when he shows kindness, the fields are drenched in downpour. Farmers look at the sky before the rains even today — the same old habit, the same old name.

The second power is — changing form. Indra can change his form whenever he wishes. Later in this book you will see that this very power was sometimes put to wrong uses too — but that story will come in its own rooms, not here. Here, just know that changing form was his power, and the right or wrong use of power is the true test of character.

And the third thing — Sahasraksha, the thousand-eyed one. They say that after the rishi Gautama's curse, a thousand marks fell upon Indra's body, which later turned into a thousand eyes. So Indra can see in every direction — forwards too, backwards too, above too, below too. (Slowly) This is an honest link: the mark of a mistake itself became one of his powers. The full story of the mistake will come in the fourth room; here only this link had to be joined, without going into detail.

Room Two — Indra's companions and weapons

And treasures — a horse, a bow, and a net

Indra has more than just the vajra and Airavata. There are other things in his treasure-house too — each with its own story.

🐴 Ucchaishrava — king of horses

Ucchaishrava is a white horse — king of horses, who came from the same churning of the ocean from which Airavata came. His pace is so swift that even the wind is left behind. In heaven he is the pride of Indra's stables.

🏹 The Vijaya bow — Vishvakarma's work

The Vijaya bow was made by Vishvakarma for Indra. Later that bow went to Parashurama, and then to Karna — but those stories are not this book's, so they are not retold here. Just know that Indra's bow too was a great weapon.

✨ Indrajal — the net in which every pearl sees all

Indrajal is one of Indra's wonderful nets, set with countless pearls — and in every pearl all the other pearls are reflected. Look at one, and you see them all. That is why later the word “Indrajal” itself came to mean magic and illusion — the art that dazzles the eyes. But how beautiful the original meaning is: everything reflected in everything else.

🌿 Pause and think — Companions and weapons

Of Indra's companion (Airavata), his weapon (the vajra), and his net (Indrajal) — which did you like most, and why? Do you too have something that is not only your strength, but also your company?

Room Three — What did he do? · The Vritra story

When the earth stayed thirsty

Now the story that made Indra the greatest hero of all.

There was a time when the rivers forgot how to flow. A giant serpent named Vritra lay coiled in the mountains, and he had held the rivers back inside the mountains themselves. The water was above, the earth below was thirsty.

Cracks split the fields. Riverbeds dried to dust. People looked at the sky and asked — when will the rain come?

Dry earth, a dry river — and eyes lifted towards the sky.

The earth seemed to call out — “Indra, give us water! Our fields are drying, our children are thirsty!”

The Vritra story — continued

The vajra rose, the storm woke

The gods were worried too, and the people too. Then everyone's prayer reached Indra. Indra raised the vajra — the vajra that the skilled craftsman Tvasta had forged for him. (Raising your voice, with passion)

Indra vowed — “The water will not stay held back. The rivers will flow again.”

Then he went and stood before Vritra. Between the mountains the giant serpent lay coiled, and behind him the held-back water boiled in anger.

The sky went black. Clouds thundered. Lightning flashed. Indra hurled the vajra — and a line of light cut the darkness. No bloodshed, no frightening sight — only light, thunder, and a breaking dam.

First one crack appeared. Then a jet of water burst out. Then, as if the mountains had opened their arms — the rivers broke free and raced downwards.

See the next page for the picture ahead — that very moment when the water was freed.

Indra's vajra, Vritra's mountain dam, and below, the freed water — a moment of light and water, with no frightening scene.
The Vritra story — the end

The earth breathed again

The water reached the fields. The rivers began to sing again. Rain fell from the sky — first drops, then downpour. (Slowly, with a sigh of relief)

People folded their hands and took Indra's name. The earth began to turn green, and the world seemed to breathe again.

That is why the Vritra story is not only a tale of battle. It is the story of this: when some great thing — water, a path, truth — is held back by someone's hand, courage is needed to free it. Indra showed that very courage.

🌿 Pause and think

Sometimes a good thing cannot reach us — like the water held back in the mountains. What good thing in your life needs to be freed from some block? And what could be the first small step to free it?

Room Three — What did he do? · Dasharajna

One king against ten kings

After Vritra comes another war, very famous in the Rigveda's songs — Dasharajna, the war of the ten kings.

The story is this: on one side was King Sudas — alone, with his small army. On the other side were ten kings together, with ten times the army. Sudas's army was small, but his trust was great — he had called upon Indra.

The war took place on the bank of the Parushni river — the river we call the Ravi today. The ten kings had dammed the river, so that by holding back the water they could trap Sudas's army. The water stopped, and Sudas's army was trapped on one side of the river — as if the Vritra story were repeating itself, but this time on a battlefield, among men.

Sudas called out — “Indra, we are few, but our trust is in you. Open the river!”

Room Three — What did he do? · Dasharajna

The dam broke, the river raced

Indra came — with the vajra, with thunder. He struck the dam. First one crack, then a jet of water, then the whole river — as if someone had opened the dam's mouth itself. The water flowed towards the ten kings' army, and their plan fell apart.

Sudas's small army attacked at that very moment, and the ten kings' great army scattered. (With passion) Numbers lost; trust won.

📜 Why did kings call upon Indra before a war?

In those days, before a war, kings prayed to Indra, because Indra was the god who breaks barriers — whether a mountain, a dam, or an enemy army. Kings did not ask Indra to fight on their behalf; they asked that the way be opened, and then they would fight themselves. Sudas did the same — he asked for a way, not for victory.

That is why Dasharajna is not only a war story. It is the story of this: when you grow weak, asking for help is not weakness — and even after help comes, the fighting is still yours to do.

The dam broke on the Parushni — Indra's vajra, the freed water, and armies on both banks.
Room Three — What did he do? · The Ravana war

When Ravana climbed up to heaven

Now a story in which Indra almost won — and yet lost. This story is from the Uttara Ramayana, from long before Rama's birth.

Ravana — king of Lanka, ten-headed, who had challenged even the gods — one day came up to heaven with his army. He wanted Indra's throne. The gods faced him, and war broke out.

At first the gods won — and this must be said plainly, because this is the story's turning point: The gods captured Ravana. Indra had almost won. Heaven's army had bound Ravana, and it seemed the war was over.

The gods said — “Ravana is captured! Heaven is safe!”

Room Three — What did he do? · The Ravana war

Meghanada — who bound Indra

But the war was not over yet. Ravana's son Meghanada — who later came to be called Indrajit — came to free his father. He was a master of illusion-warfare, fought hidden in clouds, and his rain of arrows had no answer.

Meghanada first freed his father. Then he attacked Indra and Airavata. The war went on long, but in the end Meghanada bound Indra — and took him to Lanka. The king of heaven, who had just almost won, was himself now a prisoner.

The picture is on the next page — but look carefully: Indra is bound, but not bowed. (Slowly, gravely) Dignity can remain even in defeat, and that is this picture's point. No humiliation, no mockery — only a king who is a king even in bonds.

Indra bound before Meghanada — with dignity, unbowed; Airavata behind.
Room Three — What did he do? · The Ravana war

Brahma came, and the name Indrajit was given

When news of Indra's capture reached Brahma, he himself came to Lanka. He told Ravana that Indra should be freed, and in return gave Meghanada a boon — Nikumbhila worship completed, he would be unbeatable in war.

And that very day Meghanada received a new name — Indrajit, “conqueror of Indra”. This name is the memory of his victory — and of Indra's defeat too. Stories do not hide defeat; they give it a name, so that everyone remembers.

One more link must be joined here — gently, not as a sermon. Some stories connect this defeat to Gautama's curse — the curse Indra received in the Ahalya story. That is, the fruit of an old mistake appeared much later, in a completely different war. Cause and effect — sometimes they travel very far. The full Ahalya story will come in the next room.

🌿 Pause and think — What did he do?

Indra freed the water, opened the river, and almost won one war — and yet lost a war. Is someone's greatness decided by whether he never lost at all, or by whether he stood with dignity even after losing? Do you remember a loss of your own in which you did not lose your dignity?

Room Four — Where did he go wrong?

When power grows, and pride too

This room is deliberately small. Indra's deeds are great, so the room of his mistakes should stay smaller than the room of his deeds — but this room must exist, because without it the story would be false.

The root of Indra's mistakes is one thing — pride and envy, which grow when power never hears a refusal. When everyone cheers you, when the vajra stands with you in every war, when heaven's throne is yours — then it is easy for the mind to think, “I can do whatever I wish.” And from that very moment, the mistake begins.

There are two stories in this room. The first — Ahalya's. The second — Karna's armour. Both are told at family level, briefly, and with dignity. (Slowly, gravely) No detail, no crude picture — only as much as is needed to understand the truth.

Room Four — Where did he go wrong? · Ahalya

Ahalya — a wrong deed, and its curse

There was the rishi Gautama's hermitage — quiet, holy, and full of tapasya. His wife was Ahalya. Indra entered that house by trickery — wearing the rishi's form, misusing trust. This is counted as Indra's greatest wrong deed, and this book is not hiding it.

When Gautama learned the truth, he cursed Indra — and that curse stayed on Indra's body as marks. Those same marks later turned into a thousand eyes — Sahasraksha, about whom you have already read in the companions-and-weapons room.

Here only this much needs saying: Indra broke the trust of a rishi's house, and he had to carry the fruit of it on his own body — forever. (Slowly) Even the greatest king, when he breaks someone's trust, must pay the price. In the next picture there is only this — Indra bowed, and the stern Gautama. Nothing more than that, and that is enough.

Indra bowed, before the stern Gautama — the fruit of a mistake, told with dignity.
Room Four — Where did he go wrong? · Karna

Karna's armour — a father's fear

The second story is from the Mahabharata — and it is different from the first, because here understanding Indra's heart matters too.

Karna was born wearing armour and earrings — a golden armour that was part of his very body, and which no weapon could pierce. He was a great giver: whatever anyone asked of him, he gave.

Indra's son was Arjuna — and in the great war to come, Arjuna was to face Karna. Indra feared that his son could not defeat the armour-wearing Karna. So Indra took a brahmin's form, went to Karna, and asked for his armour and earrings as a gift.

Karna gave his armour even knowing — he had recognised that this brahmin was no ordinary brahmin. The great giver kept his word, and Indra bent justice for his son's sake. (Slowly) This story does not make Indra a villain — it makes him a father who chose a wrong path for his child's sake. Both things are true together: Karna's greatness too, and Indra's mistake too.

Karna giving his golden armour to Indra in brahmin form — sunrise, a riverbank.
Room Four — Where did he go wrong? · The end

Mistakes do not cancel deeds — and deeds do not erase mistakes

So this room's final point is this — and remember it well, because this is this book's most important line:

Mistakes do not cancel deeds — and deeds do not erase mistakes.

Indra freed the water — that is true. Indra broke trust — that too is true. Indra bent justice for his son — that too is true. One truth does not make another truth false.

To know a person means just this — to see his great deeds too, and his mistakes too, together, hiding neither.

🌿 Pause and think — Where did he go wrong?

Have you ever done a wrong thing for someone of your own — like telling a lie to help someone? How did you feel at the time? And do you think a good intention makes a wrong deed right — or not?

Room Five — In later stories · Ramayana

Vali's father

Time passed. After the age of the Vedas came the age of the Ramayana — and Indra is there too, but now he is not the chief hero. Now he is at the story's edges — but without him the story is incomplete.

In the Ramayana, Indra is Vali's father. Vali was king of the vanaras — so strong that facing him was almost impossible. A part of Vali's strength came from his father Indra. Here we will not retell the story of Vali's death — that is Rama's story, not Indra's. Just know that Indra, as a father, is present in the Ramayana too — quietly, behind his son's strength.

See how Indra's form is changing: first he was the chief hero, now he is a father. Stories grow larger, and the old gods step behind the new heroes.

Room Five — In later stories · Ramayana

Matali's chariot

In the Ramayana's final war — when Rama and Ravana stood face to face — there came a moment when Rama was on foot and Ravana was on a chariot. Then Indra sent his charioteer Matali, with his divine chariot.

Matali said — “Rama, this is Indra's chariot. Climb onto it — the war must be fought on equal terms.”

Rama climbed onto that chariot, and the war was fought on equal terms. This was one of Indra's small but very great helps — he did not fight the war himself, but he made sure the war was fought with justice. The old king stood by the new hero — without asking for his own place.

And even after the war, one task of Indra's remained — it is on the next page.

Room Five — In later stories · Ramayana

A rain of nectar

The war was over. Ravana had fallen — but many vanaras who had fought on Rama's side had fallen too. Bodies lay on the earth, and even in the joy of victory there was a sadness.

Then Rama prayed to Indra — and Indra sent a rain of nectar. That rain was no ordinary rain; it was a rain of life. Wherever drops of nectar fell, the fallen vanaras rose to their feet — as if woken from sleep.

(Slowly, with a sigh of relief) At the end of the war, Indra's work was not destruction, but life. The god who once hurled the vajra was now raining nectar. This is a beautiful turn in Indra's story — power now being used to give life.

Room Five — In later stories · Mahabharata

Arjuna's father

In the Mahabharata, Indra comes again as a father — this time as Arjuna's father. Arjuna was third among the Pandavas, and the greatest archer. A part of his archery came from his father Indra.

But here too one thing is worth noting: Indra did not give Arjuna only strength, he gave him preparation too. When Arjuna needed divine weapons, Indra called him to heaven, and there he was taught the weapons. A father's work is not only to give birth — it is also to prepare.

And this is also where a link joins to the Karna story: Indra had asked for the armour for Arjuna's sake, and had also gathered weapons for Arjuna's sake. As a father, he was knocking on every door for his son's victory — rightly too, and wrongly too. This link has already been told in this book; here it is not repeated, only reminded.

Room Five — In later stories · Mahabharata

Divine weapons, and the journey to heaven

Arjuna's journey to heaven is a beautiful link in the Mahabharata. Arjuna went to heaven on Indra's chariot, there he learned music from the Gandharvas, watched the apsaras dance, and was taught divine weapons — the vajra too, and other weapons too.

When he returned, he was not only an archer — he was a warrior who had seen heaven. And when the great war came, those very weapons served him.

But here too Indra is not the chief hero. He is in the background — father, teacher, and helper. The greatest god of the Vedic age has now become a helper. This is not a fall — it is the natural change of stories. New heroes come, old gods stand behind them — and yet, without their presence, the story is incomplete.

Room Five — In later stories · Bhagavata

Govardhan — when the path of worship changed

In the Bhagavata's story, Indra appears in a completely new form — and this story is this room's greatest story, so listen to it in full.

In Vrindavan, people worshipped Indra every year — they performed yajnas, offered food, and prayed for rain. One year the boy Krishna said — “Why should we worship Indra? It is Govardhan hill that protects us, our cows protect us, our earth protects us. Worship should go to those who give to us directly.”

People agreed with Krishna. That year there was no yajna for Indra — instead Govardhan, the cows, and the earth were worshipped. Indra took this very badly. (Slowly) When a king who has always received worship gets no worship, his pride wakes up.

Room Five — In later stories · Bhagavata

Seven days of downpour, and the lifted mountain

In anger, Indra rained terribly for seven days — a downpour such as Vrindavan had never seen. Rivers overflowed, fields began to drown, cows ran in fear.

Then Krishna lifted Govardhan hill onto a single finger — as one lifts an umbrella. The village people, the cows, all came beneath the hill. For seven days the rain kept falling, and for seven days the hill stayed as a roof.

On the seventh day Indra understood — this is no ordinary boy. He stopped the rain, and himself came down. (Slowly, humbly) The king who had come in anger had now come to ask forgiveness.

Indra said — “Krishna, I rained in pride. Forgive me. You were right — worship should go to the one who gives directly.”

Govardhan held aloft, the village safe beneath it, and in the sky Indra watching, vajra in hand.
Room Five — In later stories · Bhagavata

Parijata — a second, quiet humility

After Govardhan comes another story — small, but the second link of the same humility.

Krishna's wife Satyabhama loved heaven's Parijata tree very much — the same tree you have already read about in the Amaravati room. Krishna decided to lift the tree and take it to Dwaraka.

Indra objected — the Parijata was heaven's property. The two fought, but this time Indra's anger was not as before. When he understood who Krishna was, he himself gave the tree — and blessed Satyabhama too, that the Parijata's flowers would never fade.

See the difference: at Govardhan, Indra rained in anger, and then asked forgiveness. At Parijata, he objected, but soon agreed — without seven days of downpour. (Smiling) Humility too is a habit — hard the first time, easy the second.

Krishna holding the Parijata, Indra humbly giving the tree, Satyabhama nearby.
Room Five — In later stories · The end

From chief hero to helper — and still essential

Look at this room's stories together: in the Ramayana, Indra is Vali's father, sends Matali's chariot, rains nectar. In the Mahabharata, he is Arjuna's father, gives weapons, shows heaven. In the Bhagavata, he grows angry, asks forgiveness, and then peacefully gives away the Parijata.

Nowhere is he the chief hero — but everywhere he is essential. Without his chariot, Rama's war would not be fought on equal terms; without his nectar, the vanaras would not rise; without his weapons, Arjuna would not be ready; without his forgiveness, the Govardhan story would be incomplete.

🌿 Pause and think — In later stories

Is being a helper in a story the same as being small? Have you ever played a helper's part in a friend's story — like giving them your chariot, or raining nectar for their help? How did you feel then — small, or essential?

Room Six — Where is he today?

Monsoon prayers, farmers' songs

Indra is here even today — only, not in temples, but in the rain.

In India's villages, even today when the monsoon comes late, farmers look at the sky and call upon Indra. Somewhere Indra is worshipped, somewhere only songs are sung, somewhere children pray for rain. The name is the same — Indra — and the feeling is the same as thousands of years ago: give rain, save the fields.

In cities too there is Indra — the moment lightning flashes, someone or other says, “Indra is thundering.” This is no worship, it is a habit — an old name settled into language.

A farmer said — “We do not see Indra, but we see his rain. And the rain itself is Indra.”

Room Six — Where is he today?

Indra Jatra — Nepal's festival

Every year in Nepal a great festival is celebrated — Indra Jatra. It is Kathmandu's greatest festival, celebrated in the month of Bhadrapada.

At Indra Jatra, Indra is worshipped, a chariot procession goes out, there are dances, and people give thanks for the rain. They say this festival is celebrated because Indra gave rain to the earth — and people give thanks for it even today.

There is one more thing in this festival too — the story of Indra's capture is also told, in which Indra was once caught on earth, and then released. (Smiling) So even in the festival, both Indra's defeat and his victory are remembered — exactly like this book.

Room Six — Where is he today?

Shakra — in Buddhist and Jain stories; Indraprastha — the city of his name

Indra is not only in Hindu stories. In Buddhist stories he comes by the name Shakra — king of the gods, who honours the Buddha, listens to his words, and protects him. In Jain stories too Shakra comes — at the birth and nirvana of the tirthankaras, as king of the gods.

So Indra's story has gone even beyond the boundaries of faiths. One and the same person — under different names, in different stories, but always as king of the gods.

And there is a city too, whose very name is joined to Indra — Indraprastha. In the Mahabharata, the city the Pandavas founded came to be called Indraprastha — that is, “Indra's city”. Today, Delhi stands in that very place. (In wonder) So beneath India's capital lies buried an old name — Indra's name.

Room Six — Where is he today?

Indra's names — found without even looking

📜 Indra's names — where you meet him without knowing

Indraprastha — Delhi's old name, the Mahabharata's city.
Indradhanush — the bow seen in the sky after rain, called Indra's bow.
Indrajal — the word for magic and illusion, which came from Indra's net of pearls.
Indra Jatra — Nepal's festival, celebrated every year for Indra.
Shakra — Indra's name in Buddhist and Jain stories.
Mahendra — “great Indra”, which appears in the names of many kings and places.

See — Indra may have grown fewer in temples, but he has not left language. He is in the rain, in the bow, in the festival, and in the names of cities.

🌿 Pause and think — Where is he today?

What things around you have names that come from an old story — like Indradhanush? Can you find a name near your home whose story you did not know? Next time it rains, look at the sky and take Indra's name — and think that thousands of years ago, a child was doing exactly this.

Indra on Airavata, in the sky clearing after rain, above green fields — a rain of blessing.
Final reflection

Greatness that can say — “I was wrong”

So now, when you know Indra's whole story — from birth, from heaven, from wars, from mistakes, from later stories, and right up to today — one final thing remains.

Indra's greatest greatness is not his vajra. His greatest deed is not the slaying of Vritra. His greatest thing is this, that he could say — “I was wrong.”

At Govardhan he grew angry, then asked forgiveness. At Parijata he objected, then gave the tree. In the Ahalya story he made a mistake, and bore its fruit. This is the thing that makes Indra not only powerful, but great — greatness that can own its mistake.

Questions for your listeners

1 · Now that you know Indra, what do you think — why did people sing his songs first of all?
2 · Which of Indra's stories will stay with you most — Vritra, Dasharajna, the Ravana war, Govardhan, or another? And why?
3 · Can a person be great in spite of his mistakes? What is your answer from Indra's story?
4 · If you could ask Indra one question, what would you ask?

🌿 Pause and think — final

Next time it rains, pause for a moment and think — thousands of years ago, by the rivers, someone saw exactly this same sky, and took that same name. You are the next link in that long story.

Source notes

Small notes, great stories

1 · The vajra's origin. In this book the main story is the one found in the Rigveda tradition — the craftsman Tvasta forged the vajra for Indra. There is another famous story too: that the vajra was made from the bones of the rishi Dadhichi; it will stay recorded in this book as a different story, not blended with the main story.

2 · Airavata's origin. Airavata came from the churning of the ocean and was given to Indra. This is the same churning whose story has already been told in an earlier book of this series — it is not retold here, only joined to that same event. Ucchaishrava too came from that same churning.

3 · Indra's parents. In the Rigveda's songs, Indra is called the son of Dyaus, the sky-father; in other stories, different things are found about his parents.

4 · The source of the Vritra story. The slaying of Vritra is one of the Rigveda's most famous Indra stories. In this book it is told for children simply, dramatically, and without frightening scenes; the original story's soul — held-back water, the vajra's blow, the freeing of the rivers — is kept exactly as it is.

5 · Indra — person and title. The Indra of our manvantara (the Vaivasvata manvantara) is Shakra/Purandara. Nahusha held the Indra-post temporarily and fell through pride — together with the story of kicking Agastya. Bali has been promised the Indra-post in the future Savarni manvantara; this is the same Bali whose Vamana story has already been told earlier in this series.

6 · The impermanence of heaven. Gita 9.21 — when punya fades, even heaven's dwellers return. In the Amaravati room, this very thing is said honestly.

Source notes · continued

Different forms of stories — without blending

7 · Different forms of the Ravana war. In the Uttara Ramayana tradition, the Ravana-war story is found in many forms. In this book the main story is the one in which the gods first capture Ravana, then Meghanada frees his father, binds Indra and takes him to Lanka, and at Brahma's word Indra is freed — Meghanada receiving the name Indrajit and the boon of Nikumbhila. Meghanada's victory is in all forms; the sequence of the gods first capturing Ravana is found especially in one form, and it is chosen here as the main story, not blended with other forms.

8 · From Gautama's curse to Sahasraksha. In the Ahalya story, there are many stories about the marks that fell on Indra's body after Gautama's curse; in this book they are told briefly, at family level, as “a thousand eyes” (Sahasraksha), without any crude detail. The link connecting this defeat to Gautama's curse has also been recorded, gently, as a story-tradition — not as a sermon.

9 · The Vijaya bow. The Vijaya bow was made by Vishvakarma for Indra; later it went to Parashurama and then to Karna. In this book it is only recorded as a treasure; Parashurama's and Karna's own stories are not retold here.

10 · Indrajal. The imagining of Indra's net of pearls — in which every pearl reflects all the rest — later became the source of the word “Indrajal” in the sense of magic/illusion.

11 · Art note. All the pictures in this book are original artworks, inspired by the painting style of Raja Ravi Varma — not copies of any real painting. Indra's form (mature, Indian face, moustache, golden crown, deep blue garments) and the vajra's form (thick middle cylinder, points on both sides) have been kept the same throughout the book as far as possible; wherever a small difference has remained, it is honestly recorded in the distribution note.
